satellites.name: sat_shift_details

satellites.name: sat_job_candidate_details
satellites.description: The candidate's résumé (a structured document) and the last-modified timestamp.

satellites.name: sat_business_entity_department_shift_effectivity
satellites.description: Active period of each department/shift assignment. A missing EndDate marks the current assignment.

evidence: Product.ProductNumber is 'Unique product identification number'. The vault has no product hub; its hubs cover business entity, address, contact/phone type, country, state, department, shift and job candidate.
Product.ProductID is the primary key of a Production-domain table. No existing hub has a product key or a product source entity.

Product.Name is a product name. The only existing hubs keyed on 'Name' are address type, contact type, state province, department and shift, none of them products. A shared column name is not evidence.
ProductCategory.Name is a category description. No existing hub models product categorisation.
ProductCategoryID is the primary key of ProductCategory. No existing hub models it.
ProductSubcategory.Name is a subcategory description. No existing hub matches.
ProductSubcategoryID is the primary key of ProductSubcategory. No existing hub has this key.
ProductModel.Name is a product model description. No existing hub models product models.
ProductModelID is the primary key of ProductModel. No existing hub has this key.
Culture is a language lookup (nchar(6) CultureID). The existing country_region hub uses CountryRegionCode, which is a different concept and key.
Culture.Name is a language description. No existing hub models languages or cultures.
UnitMeasure is a unit-of-measure lookup keyed by UnitMeasureCode. No existing hub models it.
Location is a manufacturing/inventory location with CostRate and Availability. It is not the postal Address modelled by hub_address (key AddressID). The shared name stem is not evidence.
Location.LocationID (smallint) is a manufacturing location key. hub_address is keyed by AddressID and models postal addresses, so there is no key match or cross-reference.
WorkOrderID identifies production work orders. No existing hub models them.
WorkOrderRouting is keyed by WorkOrderID + OperationSequence (+ ProductID). No existing construct models work order routing steps.
ScrapReason.Name is a failure description in a manufacturing lookup. No existing hub matches.
ScrapReasonID is the primary key of the ScrapReason lookup. No existing hub has it.
TransactionHistory.TransactionID identifies product transactions. TransactionHistoryArchive has the same structure but no cross-reference to any existing construct. The vault has no transaction hub.
ProductInventory is a composite-key relationship between Product and Location. No existing construct models products or locations.
ProductReviewID is the primary key of ProductReview. The reviewer is held only as a free-text name and email, with no BusinessEntityID. So there is no key match to hub_business_entity.

requirements.text: The business must be able to identify every product uniquely and unambiguously.
Each product carries a product number that is unique and serves as the natural business key used in day-to-day work.
Every product must carry a product name.
The product name is descriptive, is not guaranteed to be unique, and must not be relied on to identify a product.
The business must know, for every product, whether it is manufactured in-house or purchased from outside.
Whether a product is manufactured in-house or purchased determines whether it has a manufacturing route, a bill of materials and work orders, or arrives via purchasing.
The business must know whether each product is a salable item or not.
Reporting on the product portfolio must be able to separate salable finished goods from internal-only items.
The business must track product colour where it applies, as not all products have a colour.
The business must track product size and, separately, the unit of measure in which the size is expressed.
Product size and its unit of measure must always be read together.
The business must track product weight and, separately, the unit in which the weight is expressed.
A product weight figure is meaningless without its unit and must be read together with it.
The business must know how many days are required to manufacture a product, to support lead-time planning and promise dates.
Products are grouped into a product line, and the recognised lines are Road, Mountain, Touring and Standard.
The business must be able to report on the range, on sales performance and on manufacturing load by product line.
Products carry a class of High, Medium or Low.
The business meaning of product class is not stated in the source system and must be confirmed with the product management team before it is used as an analytical dimension.
Products carry a style of Womens, Mens or Universal.
Product style, a merchandising attribute, must be available for analysis of the range.
The business must record the standard cost of a product, which is the cost figure used for costing and margin purposes.
The business must record the list price of a product, which is the price at which it is offered for sale.
The business must be able to compare list price against standard cost to understand the margin position of each product.
The business must record a safety stock level for each product, being the minimum inventory quantity it intends to hold.
The business must record a reorder point for each product, being the inventory level at which a purchase order or work order is triggered.

The business must be able to compare actual inventory on hand against the safety stock level and the reorder point, to identify products at risk of stock-out and products where replenishment is overdue.
requirements.obj: inventory on hand against safety stock level and reorder point

requirements.text: The business must know the date from which a product became available for sale.
The business must know the date from which a product ceased to be available for sale, where that has happened; a current product has no such date.
The business must know the date on which a product was discontinued, where applicable.
Discontinuation and the end of sale availability are recorded separately and must be treated as two distinct business events, with product management to confirm the difference in meaning.
requirements.obj: difference between discontinuation and sell end

requirements.text: The business must be able to report on the active product range as at any point in time using the sell start and sell end dates.
Products are organised into a two-level classification consisting of product categories that are subdivided into product subcategories.
A product category must be identifiable by its name (its description); categories are the top level of the merchandising hierarchy.
A product subcategory must be identifiable by its name.
A product subcategory belongs to exactly one product category.
A product belongs to at most one subcategory, and not every product is placed in a subcategory.
Reporting must handle products without a subcategory gracefully rather than dropping them.
The business must be able to roll up any product-level measure, such as inventory, cost, price, transaction volume and scrap, to subcategory and then to category level.
The business must be able to identify a product model by its name.
A product belongs to at most one product model, and not every product has one.
The business must be able to group and report products by product model, the level at which design, catalogue content and manufacturing instructions are held.
Detailed catalogue information is held at product model level in a structured document format.
The business needs the product model catalogue content available for catalogue and web publication purposes.
Manufacturing instructions are held at product model level in a structured document format.
Manufacturing and quality teams must have access to the manufacturing instructions that apply to a given product model.
The level of detail that can be extracted from the structured manufacturing instruction documents must be scoped separately with the manufacturing engineering team.
requirements.obj: extractable detail of manufacturing instruction documents

requirements.text: The business maintains a library of product descriptions, which are free-text marketing descriptions of products held independently of any one product.
The business maintains a list of cultures (language and locale designations), each identified by a short culture code and carrying a descriptive name.
A product model is associated with a product description in a specific culture.
The catalogue supports multiple languages, so the same product model has different descriptions for different markets.
The business must be able to report which product models have catalogue descriptions in which cultures.
The business must be able to report which product models are missing a description in a culture the business sells into, to answer the marketing team's content-completeness question.
requirements.obj: models missing a description in a culture

requirements.text: The combination of model, description and culture is the meaningful business fact; a description is useful only when it is known which model it describes and in which language.
The business maintains a library of product photographs.
Each photograph exists in a small (thumbnail) version and a large version.
Each photograph version has its own image file and file name.
A product may have several photographs, and a photograph may be used for more than one product.
For each product, one photograph is designated the principal image.
The business must be able to identify the principal image for a product, since it is used as the lead image in the catalogue and on the web.
The business must be able to identify products that have no photograph at all.
The business must be able to identify products that have photographs but no designated principal image.
The business maintains a set of illustrations used in manufacturing instructions.
Illustrations are technical diagrams held in a structured format.
An illustration is associated with one or more product models, and a product model may have several illustrations.
The business must be able to determine which illustrations support which product models, so that manufacturing documentation can be assembled and kept complete.
The operational system holds a controlled document library organised hierarchically, with documents inside folders, and carrying approval and revision control.
The business must be able to identify each document in the library and know its title.
The business must know whether an entry in the library is a folder or an actual document.
The business must be able to reconstruct the folder structure of the document library.
Documents are organised in a hierarchy and their depth in that hierarchy is recorded.
Each document has an owner, who is an employee.
The business must be able to report on documents by owner, for example to find documents whose owner has left the company.
Employee master data is owned outside this area and must be sourced from there.
Each document carries a revision number.
The business must be able to see which revision of a document is current.
Each document is associated with an engineering change approval number.
The business must be able to trace documents to the engineering change that authorised them.
Each document has an approval status of Pending approval, Approved or Obsolete.
The business must be able to report on documents by approval status.
The business must be able to find documents pending approval and documents still in circulation that are marked obsolete.
requirements.obj: pending-approval documents and obsolete documents in circulation

requirements.text: Each document carries a file name and a file extension indicating its type, such as a word-processing document or a plain text file.
The business needs to know the document type for archiving and access purposes.
Each document has a short abstract or summary, distinct from the full document content.
The full binary document content is generally not required in analytical reporting, and its inclusion should be confirmed rather than assumed.
Documents are linked to products: a product may have several associated documents (such as assembly instructions, specifications and safety notices), and a document may apply to several products.
The business must be able to identify manufactured products that have no associated document, as a documentation-completeness check.
A product may be assembled from other products, and the business must be able to record which products are components of a given assembly.
Both sides of an assembly relationship are products in their own right.
A component in one assembly may itself be an assembly of further components, so the structure is recursive and can be several levels deep.
The business must know, for each component in an assembly, the quantity of that component needed to make one of the assembly item.
The business must know the unit of measure in which the component quantity is expressed.
requirements.obj: unit of measure of component quantity

requirements.text: The business must know how deep a component sits below its parent assembly, as the level in the bill of materials.
requirements.obj: bill of materials level of a component

requirements.text: The business must be able to explode a bill of materials down to raw components.
The business must be able to produce summary reporting of the bill of materials at a chosen level.
requirements.obj: bill of materials at a chosen level

requirements.text: Each component-in-assembly relationship carries the date the component started being used in the assembly and the date it stopped being used.
The business must be able to answer what a product was made of on a given date, not only what it is made of now.
The business must be able to identify currently active bill of materials relationships, those that have started and not yet ended, as the default view for planning and costing.
requirements.obj: currently active bill of materials relationships

requirements.text: The business must be able to see component substitutions over time, where one component stopped being used in an assembly on a date and another started, as a design change the engineering and cost teams need visibility of.
The business must be able to determine, for any component, all the assemblies it is used in (where used), in order to assess the impact of a component shortage, price change or quality problem.
requirements.obj: assemblies in which a component is used

requirements.text: The business must be able to cost an assembly from the costs of its components and the quantities required.
The business must be able to compare the built-up cost of an assembly with its recorded standard cost.
The business maintains a standard list of units of measure, each identified by a short code and carrying a descriptive name.
Units of measure are used for the quantity of a component in an assembly, the unit for a product's size, and the unit for a product's weight.
The same standard list of units of measure serves component quantity, product size and product weight.
All quantity and dimension reporting must present the unit alongside the figure.
Figures expressed in different units must never be aggregated without conversion.
Conversion factors between units of measure are not held in this system, and whether they exist anywhere in the business needs clarification.
The business operates a number of manufacturing locations, each identified by a name.
Manufacturing locations are the shop floors and work centres within the plant.
Each location has a standard hourly cost rate.
The business uses the location's standard hourly cost rate to cost the time products spend at that location.
Each location has a stated work capacity expressed in hours.
The business must be able to compare actual hours consumed at a location against its stated capacity in order to identify bottlenecks and under-used capacity.
A location serves two purposes: it is where manufacturing operations are performed and where inventory is held.
Reporting must be able to address both the manufacturing use and the inventory-holding use of the same location.
The business must know the quantity of each product held at each location.
Within a location, stock is stored in a specific shelf, and within a shelf, in a specific bin.
The business must be able to report inventory down to shelf and bin level, as used by stock-picking and stock-counting operations.
The same product may be held at several locations and a location holds many products; the business fact is the quantity of a given product at a given location, shelf and bin.
The business must be able to total inventory for a product across all locations.
The business must be able to total inventory at a location across all products.
The business must be able to value inventory by combining quantities on hand with the applicable standard cost of the product.
The operational system holds only the current inventory position, not a history of it.

To report inventory levels as at past dates, the warehouse is expected to build inventory history by capturing the inventory position over time; this is to be confirmed as a requirement with the supply chain team.
The business raises work orders to manufacture products.
Each work order must be uniquely identifiable.
Each work order must state which product is being made.
Each work order states the quantity ordered.
Each work order records the quantity actually stocked, being the good output that reached inventory.
Each work order records the quantity scrapped.
The business must be able to calculate and report a scrap rate, scrapped quantity against ordered quantity, by product, by product line, by category and over time.
Where a quantity was scrapped, the work order records a scrap reason.
The business maintains a standard list of scrap reasons, each carrying a failure description.
The business must be able to report scrap volumes and scrap costs by scrap reason in order to prioritise quality improvement effort.
requirements.obj: scrap volumes and costs by scrap reason

requirements.text: Not every work order has a scrap reason, since a work order completed without scrap has none; reporting must handle this.
Each work order records a start date, an end date and a due date.
The business must be able to report manufacturing lead time, measured from start to end of the work order.
The business must be able to report schedule adherence of work orders, measured as end date against due date.
The business must be able to identify open work orders, which are started but not ended.
The business must be able to identify work orders that are overdue against their due date.
The business must be able to report work order volume and output over time, by product and by product grouping.
Each work order is broken down into a sequence of operations.
The business must know the sequence number of each operation, since the order of performance is meaningful.
Each operation is performed at a manufacturing location.
The business must be able to report the manufacturing workload falling on each location.
Each operation carries a scheduled start date and a scheduled end date.
Each operation carries an actual start date and an actual end date, and both scheduled and actual dates must be retained.
The business must be able to compare scheduled and actual dates to report schedule adherence at operation level.
The business must be able to identify operations that are scheduled but not yet started, started but not yet finished, and completed, based on the presence of the actual dates.
Each operation records the actual resource hours consumed.
The business must be able to compare hours consumed at a location against that location's stated capacity.
Each operation carries a planned cost and an actual cost.
The business must be able to report cost variance at operation level, work order level, product level and location level.
The business must be able to combine actual resource hours with the location's standard hourly cost rate to understand how operation costs arise.
requirements.obj: actual resource hours with standard hourly cost rate

requirements.text: The business must be able to reconcile the cost derived from hours and hourly rate against the recorded actual operation cost.
requirements.obj: derived cost against recorded actual cost

requirements.text: The business must be able to roll up all operations of a work order to give the total manufactured cost for that work order.
The business must be able to compare the total manufactured cost of a work order against the standard cost of the product manufactured.
Each operation identifies the product being manufactured as well as the work order.
The product on an operation is expected to agree with the product on its work order, and any disagreement must be flagged as a data quality issue.
requirements.obj: product disagreement between operation and work order

requirements.text: The business maintains a history of standard cost for each product, with a start date and an end date defining the period during which each cost applied.
The business must be able to determine the standard cost that applied to a product on any given date, not just the current cost.
requirements.obj: standard cost at a given date

requirements.text: The current standard cost period is the one with no end date.
The business must be able to identify the currently applicable standard cost for every product.
The business must be able to report cost movements over time, showing how the standard cost of a product, product line or category has changed and by how much.
The current product record also carries a standard cost figure, which is expected to agree with the currently applicable entry in the cost history.
The business must reconcile the product record's standard cost against the current cost history entry and report any disagreement as a data quality issue.
requirements.obj: product standard cost against cost history

requirements.text: Historic transactions must be valued using the cost applicable at the time of the transaction, not today's cost, wherever margin or manufacturing cost is analysed over a period.
The business maintains a history of list price for each product, with a start date and an end date defining the period during which each price applied.
The business must be able to determine the list price that applied to a product on any given date.
requirements.obj: list price at a given date

requirements.text: The current list price period is the one with no end date.
The business must be able to identify the currently applicable list price for every product.
The business must be able to report price movements over time, including the frequency, size and direction of price changes by product, product line and category.
The current product record also carries a list price, which is expected to agree with the currently applicable entry in the price history.
The business requires a reconciliation between the product record's list price and the current price history entry.
requirements.obj: product list price against price history

requirements.text: The business must be able to analyse margin over time by combining the list price applicable on a date with the standard cost applicable on the same date.
Cost history and price history are maintained independently and their periods do not necessarily align, so margin analysis must handle overlapping but non-identical periods.
Every movement of stock is recorded as an inventory transaction, forming the movement history behind the current inventory position.
The business must be able to identify each inventory transaction uniquely.
Each inventory transaction states the product involved.
Each inventory transaction states the quantity moved.
Each inventory transaction states the date and time it occurred.
Each inventory transaction states its type, which is one of work order, sales order or purchase order.
The business must be able to separate manufacturing movements, outbound sales movements and inbound purchase movements.
Each inventory transaction refers to the originating order and to the specific line on that order, which is a work order, sales order or purchase order depending on the transaction type.
The order reference on a transaction is ambiguous on its own and must always be read together with the transaction type to know which kind of order is meant.
The business must be able to trace a stock movement back to the document that caused it.
Each inventory transaction carries an actual cost.
The business must be able to value stock movements at the cost actually applied.
The business must be able to report cost of goods manufactured, sold and purchased on the basis of actual cost.
requirements.obj: cost of goods manufactured, sold and purchased

requirements.text: The business must be able to reconcile the net effect of transactions for a product against the current inventory quantity held for that product, as a data quality and stock-accuracy control.
requirements.obj: net transactions against current inventory quantity

requirements.text: Inventory transactions do not record a location, so movement history is available at product level but not at location level.
If location-level movement analysis is required, the missing location on transactions is a gap that needs to be raised with the operational system owners.
The business must be able to report transaction volume and value over time, by product, product grouping and transaction type.
Older inventory transactions are moved out of the live operational store into an archive.
The archive holds the same information as the live store: transaction identifier, product, order reference and line, date, type, quantity and actual cost.
For long-run historical analysis, the business must be able to see live and archived transactions as one continuous history.
requirements.obj: live and archived transactions as one history

requirements.text: Reporting that covers a multi-year period but looks only at the live store would silently under-report.
The rule that governs when a transaction is archived must be clarified with the operational system owners.
A transaction must exist in exactly one of the live and archive stores at any time and must never be counted twice; this needs confirmation with the operational system owners.
Customers submit reviews of products.
The business must be able to identify each review.
The business must know which product each review relates to.
Each review records the name of the reviewer.
Each review records the e-mail address of the reviewer.
Each review records the date the review was submitted.
Each review carries a rating on a scale of one to five, with five the highest.
Each review carries free-text comments from the reviewer.
The business must be able to report average rating and review volume by product, by product model, by subcategory and by category.
The business must be able to track how ratings move over time.
The business must be able to identify products with consistently low ratings so that quality and product management can act on them.
The business must be able to relate poorly rated products to their scrap and manufacturing cost history.
requirements.obj: poorly rated products to scrap and manufacturing cost history

requirements.text: Reviewer e-mail addresses are personal data, and any use of review data in reporting must respect data protection obligations.
How reviewer identity is handled in analytical reporting must be agreed with the data protection officer before review data is published in reports.
Reviewers are identified only by name and e-mail address, with no link to the customer master.
Whether a reviewer can or should be matched to a known customer is an open question for the customer data owners and is out of scope.
Every record in the operational system carries the date and time it was last updated.
The business must be able to use the last-updated date and time to understand the currency of the data and to detect records that have not been maintained.
The business must be able to report the as-at date of any figure presented, so users know what point in time a report reflects.
Analysis of past periods must use the bill of materials, standard cost and list price values that applied at the time.
requirements.obj: historical bills of materials, standard costs and list prices

requirements.text: Past-period analysis must not be silently restated when a cost, price or assembly structure changes.
A product may have no subcategory, no model, no photograph, no document, no review and no bill of materials, and reporting must treat these absences as legitimate business situations, not errors.
Reporting must still be able to report on absent optional relationships as completeness gaps where that is the question being asked.
The relationships between products and documents, products and photographs, models and illustrations, and models and descriptions by culture are many-to-many.
Each many-to-many association is a business fact in its own right and must be retained as such.

The document owner reference to an employee, and the inventory transaction references to sales orders and purchase orders, point outside the production area and must be able to join up with the human resources, sales and purchasing areas of the warehouse when those are built.
Until the human resources, sales and purchasing areas are built, the cross-area references can only be reported as identifiers.

Some content is held as structured documents or binary content rather than simple fields: catalogue descriptions, manufacturing instructions, illustration diagrams, photograph images and full document content.
What structured and binary content is needed for business reporting, and at what level of detail, must be agreed with marketing and manufacturing engineering rather than assumed.
requirements.obj: structured and binary content needed for reporting

requirements.text: Technical record identifiers in the operational system that have no business meaning must not surface in business reporting.

business_keys.rationale: REQ-002 explicitly states the product number is unique and is the natural business key used day to day; it satisfies uniqueness and business recognition, and REQ-001 requires unambiguous identification. Every product carries one, so it is non-nullable.

System-generated surrogate used for joins in the source; REQ-053-3 says technical identifiers with no business meaning must not surface in business reporting. Weak as a business key compared with the product number (REQ-002).
REQ-003 requires every product to have a name, but REQ-004 states the name is not guaranteed unique and must not be used to identify a product. It fails the uniqueness criterion.

REQ-033 states a product category must be identifiable by its name (description); the name is business-recognised and top-level hierarchy members are stable. Uniqueness is implied but not explicitly stated.
Surrogate source identifier with no business meaning (REQ-053-3); the name (REQ-033) is the business identifier.
REQ-034 states a product subcategory must be identifiable by its name. Each subcategory belongs to exactly one category (REQ-035). Uniqueness is implied rather than stated.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-053-3); the name (REQ-034) is the business identifier.
REQ-039 states the business must identify a product model by its name; it is business-recognised and mandatory for identification. Uniqueness is implied but not explicitly stated.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-053-3); the name (REQ-039) is the business identifier.
REQ-002-2 states each culture is identified by a short culture code. It is a stable, business-recognised code and every culture carries one.
REQ-002-2 gives the culture a descriptive name, but the code is the stated identifier; the name is descriptive only.
REQ-056 states each unit of measure is identified by a short code and carries a descriptive name. The code is stable, unique and used across component quantity, size and weight (REQ-057, REQ-058).
REQ-001-3 states each manufacturing location is identified by a name, and the business recognises locations by name. Uniqueness is implied by the identification statement.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-053-3); the location name (REQ-001-3) is the stated identifier.

REQ-019-3 requires each work order to be uniquely identifiable and REQ-018-3 says the business raises work orders. WorkOrderID is the only identifier listed for work orders and it is unique and non-null, but it is system-generated, so it scores lower than an explicit business-assigned number would.

REQ-035-3 and REQ-036-3 say each work order is broken into operations whose sequence number is meaningful, so the sequence number is unique within a work order. REQ-051-2 adds that an operation also identifies the product, which should agree with the work order's product.

REQ-026-3 says the business maintains a standard list of scrap reasons, each carrying a failure description. The requirements state no explicit identifier, so the name is the best business-facing candidate.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-053-3). It is a weak key, though it is the only other identifier available for the standard list (REQ-026-3).

REQ-002-4 requires each inventory transaction to be uniquely identifiable, and REQ-019-4 lists the transaction identifier as held in both live and archive stores. REQ-023-4 says a transaction exists in exactly one store, so the same key supports a single continuous history (REQ-020-4).

REQ-012-3 states the business fact is the quantity of a given product at a given location, shelf and bin. REQ-009-3 and REQ-010-3 support this combination as the identifier. It is a composite of product and location keys, and it is not a hub-level object on its own.

REQ-025-4 requires each review to be identifiable, but the requirements give no natural identifier. Reviewers are identified only by name and e-mail (REQ-038-4), and these are personal data (REQ-036-4), so the system-generated ID is the only practical key. It is a weak surrogate.

REQ-041-2 and REQ-042-2 say both sides of an assembly relationship are products. REQ-049 says each relationship carries a start date. Together these identify a component-in-assembly relationship over time.
System-generated surrogate with no business meaning (REQ-053-3). The natural combination of assembly, component and start date is preferred.

REQ-021-2 requires each document in the hierarchical library (REQ-020-2) to be identifiable. DocumentNode is the hierarchy position used to rebuild the folder structure (REQ-023-2, REQ-024-2). No explicit business identifier is stated, so confidence is moderate.
System-generated globally unique identifier with no business meaning (REQ-053-3). It is a weak fallback key.
REQ-021-2 says the business must know each document's title. Titles are descriptive, and nothing states they are unique or stable, so the title is a poor key.

REQ-001-2 describes a library of free-text descriptions held independently of any product, with no natural identifier. REQ-007-2 says the model, description and culture combination is the meaningful fact. The surrogate is a weak fallback.
REQ-008-2 describes a library of photographs with no natural identifier stated; file names (REQ-010-2) are not described as unique. The surrogate is a weak fallback key.
REQ-016-2 describes a set of illustrations with no natural identifier in the requirements. The surrogate is a weak fallback key.

# ADR-0001: Data Vault model derived from requirements

**Status:** Proposed
**Date:** 2026-11-15
**Decision makers:** Vault-Agent (generated) — pending human review

## Context

This model was derived automatically by the Vault-Agent pipeline from 229 requirement(s) and 29 business key candidate(s). It records the Data Vault 2.0 structures the modeler chose and traces each back to the requirements that justify it.

## Decision

Model the following Data Vault 2.0 structures.

### Hubs (16)

- **hub_product** — business key `ProductNumber`. A product, identified by its unique product number. _(requirements: REQ-001, REQ-002, REQ-004)_
- **hub_product_category** — business key `Name`. Top level of the merchandising hierarchy, identified by name. _(requirements: REQ-032, REQ-033)_
- **hub_product_subcategory** — business key `Name`. Second level of the merchandising hierarchy, identified by name. _(requirements: REQ-032, REQ-034)_
- **hub_product_model** — business key `Name`. Product model, identified by name; the level for design, catalogue and instructions. _(requirements: REQ-039, REQ-041)_
- **hub_culture** — business key `CultureID`. Language/locale designation identified by culture code. _(requirements: REQ-002-2)_
- **hub_product_description** — business key `ProductDescriptionID`. Free-text marketing description held in a library independent of products. _(requirements: REQ-001-2)_
- **hub_product_photo** — business key `ProductPhotoID`. Product photograph in the photo library. _(requirements: REQ-008-2)_
- **hub_illustration** — business key `IllustrationID`. Technical illustration used in manufacturing instructions. _(requirements: REQ-016-2, REQ-017-2)_
- **hub_document** — business key `DocumentNode`. Entry (document or folder) of the controlled document library, identified by its hierarchy node. _(requirements: REQ-020-2, REQ-021-2, REQ-023-2)_
- **hub_unit_measure** — business key `UnitMeasureCode`. Standard unit of measure identified by short code. _(requirements: REQ-056, REQ-057, REQ-058)_
- **hub_location** — business key `Name`. Manufacturing location / work centre, also an inventory-holding location, identified by name. _(requirements: REQ-001-3, REQ-002-3, REQ-007-3)_
- **hub_work_order** — business key `WorkOrderID`. Work order raised to manufacture a product. _(requirements: REQ-018-3, REQ-019-3)_
- **hub_work_order_operation** — business key `work_order_operation`. An operation of a work order, identified by work order and operation sequence. _(requirements: REQ-035-3, REQ-036-3)_
- **hub_scrap_reason** — business key `Name`. Standard scrap reason (failure description). _(requirements: REQ-025-3, REQ-026-3)_
- **hub_inventory_transaction** — business key `TransactionID`. Inventory transaction (stock movement), from live and archive stores as one continuous history. Integrated from 2 source(s): TransactionHistory.TransactionID, TransactionHistoryArchive.TransactionID; canonical staging key column `TRANSACTIONID`. _(requirements: REQ-001-4, REQ-002-4, REQ-018-4, REQ-019-4, REQ-020-4, REQ-023-4)_
- **hub_product_review** — business key `ProductReviewID`. Customer review of a product. _(requirements: REQ-024-4, REQ-025-4)_

### Links (17)

- **link_product_product_subcategory** — connects hub_product, hub_product_subcategory. Product placed in (at most one) subcategory. _(requirements: REQ-036, REQ-038)_
- **link_product_subcategory_product_category** — connects hub_product_subcategory, hub_product_category. Subcategory belongs to exactly one category. _(requirements: REQ-035, REQ-038)_
- **link_product_product_model** — connects hub_product, hub_product_model. Product belongs to at most one product model. _(requirements: REQ-040, REQ-041)_
- **link_product_size_unit_measure** — connects hub_product, hub_unit_measure (size). Unit of measure in which the product size is expressed. _(requirements: REQ-010, REQ-011, REQ-057)_
- **link_product_weight_unit_measure** — connects hub_product, hub_unit_measure (weight). Unit of measure in which the product weight is expressed. _(requirements: REQ-012, REQ-013, REQ-057)_
- **link_product_model_description_culture** — connects hub_product_model, hub_product_description, hub_culture. A product model's description in a specific culture. Unit of work: ProductModel + ProductDescription + Culture. _(requirements: REQ-003-2, REQ-004-2, REQ-005-2, REQ-006-2, REQ-007-2, REQ-047-3, REQ-048-3)_
- **link_product_product_photo** — connects hub_product, hub_product_photo. Many-to-many association of products and photographs. _(requirements: REQ-011-2, REQ-012-2, REQ-014-2, REQ-047-3)_
- **link_product_model_illustration** — connects hub_product_model, hub_illustration. Illustrations supporting product models. _(requirements: REQ-018-2, REQ-019-2, REQ-047-3)_
- **link_product_document** — connects hub_product, hub_document. Documents associated with products (many-to-many). _(requirements: REQ-039-2, REQ-040-2, REQ-047-3)_
